1:
When the sickness fell is disputed. Gill reports that interpreters are not agreed whether it came before or after the destruction of the Assyrian army, that Jarchi and others place it three days before that ruin, and that Josephus puts it after the deliverance. Calvin comes down for after the siege was raised, arguing from silence: had Hezekiah been ill during it the prophet would not have passed that over, since he records the king spreading a letter before the Lord in the temple, which does not suit a man under heavy sickness. Ellicott takes the other side, since the deliverance of the city is spoken of a few verses later as still future; and he concludes that we have no ground for supposing the illness an attack of the plague that destroyed the army.

Henry reads the opening for its lessons. Neither greatness nor goodness exempts a man from the arrests of sickness and death; he is struck with a mortal disease in the midst of his triumph over a ruined army, which teaches us to rejoice with trembling. On the command to set the house in order he adds the heart to the house, and observes that being ready for death makes it come never the sooner but much the easier, since those fit to die are most fit to live. He notes that the king prayed in sickness as in danger, calling prayer a salve for every sore, personal or public. Ellicott handles the same phrase as idiom, literally give orders to thy house, meaning make thy will; and he takes the announcement as a striking illustration of the conditional character of prophecy, like the warning that a great city should fall in three days. He suggests the prophet may have been consulted half as prophet and half as physician; and he wonders whether the words carry a hint of disappointment at the reign, since amid all the magnificence there was that in the inner house of the soul which required ordering.

Turning to the wall gets its fullest treatment from Clarke, who explains it from eastern furniture. The corner is the place of honour; he cites travellers who found a sheikh sitting in the corner of his tent, and explains the custom by the fact that whoever sits there is separated from the company. The royal couch standing so, the king had only to turn on either side to face the wall and withdraw from those attending him. Gill allows two readings, the wall of the bedchamber so that his tears might not be seen, or the wall of the temple, toward which good men looked when they prayed. Calvin insists that the attitude in itself is immaterial but that what it secures is not: we are naturally unsteady and easily drawn aside, so that everything which would lead us aside ought to be removed.

The prayer divides them most sharply. Ellicott finds in it, devout as it is, a tone of self-satisfaction: the king rests on what he had done by way of religious reformation and asks what he has done to deserve an untimely death. His concession is memorable, that the tears were probably less egotistic than the words and therefore more prevailing. Calvin denies the charge outright. Hezekiah is not pleading merit but fortifying himself against a temptation, since the severity of the chastisement might have persuaded him that God had cast him off. Here the king is meeting a craftiness that overwhelms believers with despair under the pretence of humility. Gill offers a plainer motive, that a man cut off in the prime of his days would be thought guilty of some enormous crime. Keil and Delitzsch set the passage beside its parallel, marking where the other account adds a title for the king, promises a cure by the third day, and grounds the deliverance of the city on a name.
4:
Calvin dwells on the interval between the sentence and its reversal. The prophet had departed leaving the sting in the wound, and the glad tidings were not brought until the king had struggled long and perceived himself utterly ruined; being kept in darkness by the hiding of the face of God was itself a severe trial of faith. Yet while consolation was withdrawn, his faith was not so extinguished as to emit no sparks, since by a secret influence groans that could not be uttered rose out of the gulf of his sorrow. From this Calvin draws a rule: God hears believers in the day of trouble, but his favour does not shine on them all at once, being held back until they are sincerely humbled. If a king so eminent in piety had to be brought almost to anguish before he was moved to seek that favour, we should not wonder when we are left agitated by fears and answered later than we asked.

The reversal raises the harder question, and Calvin states the objection plainly. It seems strange that God, having pronounced a sentence, should soon after revoke it as if by repentance, when nothing is more at variance with his nature than a change of purpose. His answer is that death was threatened but not decreed, the threat being the instrument by which the king was tested; the promise that follows is not a reversal but the end for which the threat was uttered.

Calvin notices a change of style in the second message that carries the whole comfort. When the prophet came to strike terror, the bare name of God was enough, the king being summoned as a criminal to a judgment seat; now that he comes with consolation he distinguishes God by an honourable title, which points out the cause of the grace, a regard to the covenant made with the ancestor named. Nothing, he says, is harder than for hearts alarmed by a conviction of anger to be raised to favourable hope, and so the confirmation was necessary: the king, ruined in himself, is reminded of a promise that kings of that seed would reign as long as the sun and moon shine. That, in his phrase, was the plank the king seized and by which he escaped shipwreck. David is named not as a private person but as an eternal king, eternal not in himself but in his seed.

The promise of deliverance for the city reopens the question of when the sickness fell. Gill takes the verse at face value and infers that it must have come while the Assyrian was near the city and about to besiege it, unless the words were meant to secure the people against the fear of his returning. Those who place the illness during the siege rest on the claim that otherwise the promise would be superfluous; but there is little force in that, since the invader might have mustered a fresh army later, so that any report was reason enough for alarm. The promise is therefore not superfluous, since along with life it grants protection the king would not otherwise have had.

Ellicott uses the fifteen years as a fixed point, dating the illness by the received reckoning; and he is careful that the danger from Assyria implied in the following verse does not point to the famous invasion, since an earlier attack may have caused a general alarm. Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch both work from the parallel account. Clarke observes that the other copy adds a clause grounding the defence of the city on two names, and that the sentence seems abrupt without it; Keil and Delitzsch set out the same collation, marking where the parallel adds the promise of a cure by the third day and where it turns the pledge into a question.
7:
Calvin begins with a point of arrangement, that the fuller history records in order how the king asked for a sign and had it granted, which this prophet mentions only at the end of the chapter; it is no new thing, he says, for Hebrew writers to reverse a narrative. From that he distinguishes two kinds of sign, those God gives unprompted and those he grants on request. Since signs are meant to aid our weakness he does not usually wait to be asked, and Calvin lists those appointed unasked, the tree of life, the bow in heaven, the cloud and pillar of fire, the serpent of brass and the passover; against these he sets the rarer case of Gideon, given one sign and then another on asking. Because that case is rare, he warns, it should not be produced as an example; and to the objection that asking a sign insults God, he answers that a weak faith is not to be called unbelief.

Ellicott tells the fuller story from the parallel: the king asks, is offered his choice whether the shadow shall go forward or back, and with something of a childlike simplicity takes the harder option. He reconstructs the instrument too. The dial of Ahaz was probably copied, like his altar, from foreign art, the earliest mention of a sun-clock being ascribed by Herodotus to another people; and since the Hebrew word means steps, it seems to have been an obelisk standing on a flight of them, each marking an hour or half hour. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the name belonged to a dial he had erected, but note that the same word can mean a step or a degree, so that a dial-plate with a gnomon is also possible.

What actually moved is the sharpest disagreement. Gill holds that the sun itself went back, since the next clause says so expressly, since it is not easy to conceive how the shadow could retreat unless the sun did, and since a change confined to one dial would never have drawn the notice and inquiry of other nations. Clarke takes the other side, observing that in the parallel history there is no mention of the sun but only of the going back of the shadow, which might be effected by a supernatural refraction; he adds that the versions point one word differently. Ellicott holds the same view and presses it further. The phenomenon seems as curiously limited as the darkness at the crucifixion, since there was no lengthening of the day elsewhere; at Babylon nothing of the kind had been observed, and investigating it was one ostensible purpose of the embassy that came later. He grants that inquiring into the causation of a miracle is almost a contradiction in terms, but offers as most probable an exceedingly circumscribed refraction, a prolonged afterglow reviving the brightness of the day, which would produce just this effect for anyone watching the steps.

Calvin is less interested in the mechanism than in the fitness of the sign, which resembles its event: as it is in the power of God to change the hours of the day, so it is in his power to lengthen a life. He anticipates the question why the shadow did not go back as many degrees as there were years added, and answers that the dial carried only twelve. The number need not trouble anyone; the correspondence is enough.

He ends by dismissing a story built on the verse, that the day on which Ahaz died had been shortened by ten hours as a punishment, and that what was taken from him was restored here. Calvin objects that there is no history of any such thing, that it is destitute not only of evidence but of probability, and that nothing is said here about that death, but only about the dial he had made.
9:
Henry asks first why a new composition was needed. The king might have taken some of the psalms of his father and found many pertinent ones, and had appointed the Levites to praise the Lord with those words; but the occasion was extraordinary, and with his heart full he would not confine himself to compositions already in hand, though of divine inspiration, but offered his affections in his own words, which Henry calls the most natural and genuine way. He asks too why it was written rather than spoken, and answers that the king meant to review it, for the reviving of the good impressions the providence had made, and to leave it recommended to others for the like occasion. From that he draws a list of the writings proper after a sickness: a memorial of the affliction and of the frame of our hearts under it, a record of the thoughts we had while ill, a memorial of the mercies of a sick bed, a thanksgiving, and a sure covenant sealed and given under our hands that we will never return again to folly.

He then turns the excellence of the writing against its author. The later history records that he rendered not again according to the benefit done to him; the impressions should never have worn off, and yet they did. Henry ends with a phrase that does the work of a paragraph, that thanksgiving is good but thanksliving is better.

Calvin values the writing for another reason. The sacred history gives no account of it, yet it deserved recording, since the king was unwilling to pass over in silence or bury in forgetfulness so remarkable a blessing. In this he shows what all believers owe when God exerts his power for them unusually: they should make their gratitude known not to contemporaries only but to posterity, and this song stands as a public record, as many psalms were composed after great deliverances. Calvin presses the duty hardest on the prominent, holding that the more eminent a man is and the higher his station, the more he is bound to consider himself placed by God upon a theatre; and he guards the point at once, warning men of every rank against the ambition that professes to imitate such examples while magnifying its own name more than the name of God.

Whether the king wrote it has been doubted, and the doubt is dismissed briskly. The conjecture that the prophet dictated the psalm is called perfectly gratuitous, since it is no stranger that this king should compose a psalm than that he should direct a collection of proverbs, and it would have been far stranger if a man so like David in spirit had not followed his example in devotional composition. Ellicott argues the same from what is known of him: the culture the psalm implies is what might be expected of one trained by this prophet, who had restored and organised the worship of the temple and addressed both Levites and soldiers as a preacher, speaking to their heart. He adds that the hymn will be found to echo the book of Job as well as the earlier psalms.

Two practical notes frame the song. Clarke warns that the parallel book deserts us here, the song not being inserted there, and that another copy would have been of great service, since the passage is very obscure, not only from its concise poetical style but because the text is probably corrupt; the manuscripts and the ancient versions, he says, will carry us through some of the difficulties. Ellicott raises a question of arrangement, that the two verses at the end of the chapter about the poultice and the sign would seem to have their right place before the psalm rather than after it. Gill notes that two versions call the piece a prayer, and prefers the Targum.
10:
The opening phrase is read three ways. Gill takes it as a cutting off in allusion to the weaver web, notes that the king was then about thirty-nine, and reports that a death before fifty was called by the Jews a cutting off. Keil and Delitzsch prefer in quiet of my days, meaning in the midst of the quiet course of a healthy life. Ellicott rejects the first on a point of fact, since the complaint could not come in the quiet of his life; he prefers the dividing point, the half-way house of life, observing that a man of thirty-nine falls between thirty-five and forty, the moieties of the seventy and eighty of the psalm, and comparing the opening line of Dante.

Ellicott calls the gates of the grave an image of the same kind. The place of the dead is conceived, as in Dante, as a great city, and therefore has gates, which become the symbol of its power; the residue of years assumes a normal span of seventy on which a sufferer might have counted.

Calvin faces the objection that the song raises. It is a very melancholy piece, containing complaints rather than prayers, the singer so oppressed that he was weary with groaning and did not venture to rise into prayer; and it may be thought strange that a man should be so attached to a fading life. What purpose, then, was served by committing such stormy passions to writing? His answer is that nothing could be more advantageous to us than the picture of a man overwhelmed with grief painted to the life. He meant to make his weakness known, to give a lesson of humility to the children of God, and to magnify the grace that had brought a ruined man out of the lowest depths.

On the fear of seeing God no more the readings pull apart. Ellicott takes the words as characteristic of the cheerless dimness of Hebrew thoughts of death; for this king it was the outward worship of the temple that he could not bear to lose, since the perceptions of the life after death would be spectral and shadowy like the dead themselves. Gill softens it, taking the loss as of this world only, since in the other he should see more clearly and face to face. Calvin concedes the difficulty, that this man seems to confine the seeing of God to the present life. The message of vengeance struck him as a deprivation of fatherly love, and with his attention fixed on the curse he could not rise so quickly to heaven. Godly minds, Calvin says, are sometimes overclouded, so that consolation is suppressed for a time while it still remains and afterwards shows itself.

The last image draws divergent comment. Ellicott reads the departing home as the body, and the shepherd tent as the type of a transitory dwelling; the weaving he takes of a man who had been weaving the web of his life and now must roll it up, finished before its time, and he detects a tone of reverence in the impersonal form of the statement, since the sufferer will not name the author of his trouble. Clarke turns the same tent the other way and asks whether the removal from one state to another, as a shepherd shifts his tent, is not a strong intimation of belief in a future state. Calvin notices that the cause of death is ascribed now to the man and now to God: where he speaks as author he does not complain but accuses himself, as if to say he had cut this thread for himself and was alone the cause of his death; and yet the same act is ascribed to God, since although we give him grounds for dealing severely it is he who judges and inflicts.
13:
The first verb is read three ways, and the difference changes the temper of the line. Gill takes it as reckoning, the sick man fixing it in his mind that he could live no longer than till morning, and notes that by the accents the clause should run that he reckoned till morning as a lion. Clarke prefers roaring, since one version read the verb proper to a lion, a word often applied to the deep groaning of men in sickness, and observes that the Masoretes divide the sentence so as to draw the lion into the first clause. Ellicott rejects both and renders it that he quieted himself, throwing himself into the calm submission of a weaned child; and he makes the pathos turn on the morning, which brought a fresh access of suffering, life prolonged only for renewed agony.

Calvin draws a chronological inference. Since the previous verse expected immediate death and this one waits again through a night, the king must have lain at least two days under the disease. He glosses the life of a day by the Greek saying that man is the creature of a day, and defends the harshest image in the song. That God should be compared to a lion ought not to be thought strange, though he is naturally gracious; we cannot be aware of that gentleness while we have provoked him, and no fierceness in any wild beast strikes the terror we feel at the bare mention of his name. This is just, Calvin says, since his chastisements must have power to cast us down to hell itself. Wesley reads it simply, as a night without rest in which the thoughts were presaging that God would break him to pieces.

The birds are handled as a description of the voice. Ellicott identifies them strictly as the swift, the crane and the dove, each with its own note, and takes them for the cries of pain and the low suppressed wail of the sufferer. Gill hears both extremes in them, loud when the pain was acute and very low through weakness, like the twittering of a swallow; and he mentions the view that the birds describe the prayers themselves, uttered not in words but in groans.

Calvin builds his most useful observation on that. The pain had taken away the voice, so that nothing was heard but indistinct groaning; and yet such a sound is heard by God, who beholds the heart and listens to sighs even when the throat is choked with grief. Such sighs, he says, are more powerful than plain words, provided the Spirit is present who produces the groanings that cannot be uttered; and no believer fails to find, when his heart is weighed down by sorrow, that in prayer he either stammers or is almost dumb.

The last clause carries a dispute of its own. Ellicott renders it be surety for me, and finds behind it the figure of Death as a creditor pressing for payment, though in another sense only the minister of God; the appeal is to the judge who is also the accuser, asking him to go bail for the accused. Clarke would render it contend for me instead, taking the verb in the sense established by the naming of a well after a quarrel. Calvin argues about the eyes instead, noting that the rendering my eyes are weakened will not agree with the phrase on high, since the sense of lifting belongs to a different root; he grants that the weakened reading has been followed by almost all, but prefers the simpler sense, that though the eyes were nearly worn out the man did not cease looking upward. Keil and Delitzsch mark the turn of the poem here, where the promise of help is described, the new life it put into him, and its fulfilment in turning his sufferings into salvation.
15:
The opening question is taken by most as an exclamation of joy. Ellicott says words simply fail to express the wonder and gratitude of a man rescued so suddenly, and Gill has him at a loss what to render for such benefits. Calvin dissents. The complaint is still running: the man speaks as those do who are overcome by grief, that life and death are in the hand of God and it is useless to protest. Calvin generalises the point: we never cease to complain until we are restrained by fear of that power.

What follows divides them further. Ellicott would render it that he should walk at ease upon the trouble of his soul, and notes that the verb here means the journey of life, taken with calm and considerate steps; the received version, he says, wrongly suggests a lifelong bitterness. Clarke keeps that sense, translating it that through the rest of his years he will reflect on this bitterness of soul.

On what men live by there is agreement. Gill takes it of the word of God and not bread only, of the promise and the power performing it; Ellicott the same, glossing the second clause as wholly through them; Wesley infers that it is not strange one word of God should have brought him back from the jaws of death. Calvin finds the concise style responsible for several interpretations and rejects the commonest, that others shall lengthen their life as he has, which he calls forced. Supplying a relative, he makes the sense that the favour will be acknowledged not by that generation only but by posterity, and this magnifies it, since it will remain engraven on remembrance and be reckoned a kind of resurrection. Clarke adds that afflictions tending to a speedy death not unfrequently become the means both of saving the soul and of lengthening the life.

Keil and Delitzsch mark this as the strophe in which he rejoices in the preservation of life and promises praise. The hardest clause is the one about peace and bitterness, and here the majority stands against the received sense. Gill will not have it that a bitter affliction came in place of expected peace, and offers instead that the speaker is now at peace though he had been in great bitterness, or that the bitterness itself has been turned into peace. Clarke renders it that his anguish is changed into ease, notes that the play on words is a figure this prophet frequently admits, and says that here it perfectly clears up the great obscurity of the passage. Ellicott is the most emphatic: the received version reads like a retrospect of the change from health to suffering, whereas the words express the opposite, that it was for his peace, meaning his salvation, that the bitterness was bitter to him. Calvin alone keeps the older reading, that sudden calamities disturb us more than gradual ones, that the disease was the more insupportable for seizing him while he enjoyed quiet, and that the saints sometimes rely too much on prosperity.

The last clause is a matter of what the text does not say. Ellicott points out that the words rendered delivered it are not in the Hebrew at all, and that while a slight change would supply them, the phrase as it stands is singularly suggestive: thou hast loved me out of the pit of corruption, the love of God being thought of as in itself the deliverance. Calvin reaches the same place by weighing the verb, which can mean either to love or to wish; nothing needs to be understood, since the line runs perfectly as it stands, that God embraced the soul with favour and kindness. Ellicott closes by tying the two halves of the verse together, that the bodily healing here was the pledge and earnest of the spiritual, as it was in the miracles.
18:
The denial that the dead praise God is handled carefully. Gill limits it to the body, since those under the power of the grave cannot celebrate God with their bodily organs, though their souls may praise him in heaven. Wesley limits it to the audience, since the dead cannot glorify the name among men upon earth. Ellicott takes it as a mark of an older view, a dim shadow world in which there are no psalms of thanksgiving and no loud hallelujahs, and holds that the notion of spiritual energies intensified after death belongs to a later and better lit immortality.

Calvin faces the difficulty and grants it. The language is too exclusive, since the death of believers declares the glory of God no less than their life, and after death they do not cease to proclaim his praises along with the angels. His explanation is that the king was not in a state to feel it. The terror was not produced by death alone, since the same man, when his life was actually ended, yielded willingly; what he grieved over was that by his own sins he had shut himself out of life. Calvin generalises it into a description of despair: those struck by that thunderbolt cannot celebrate the praises of God either living or dead, but being overwhelmed must be dumb.

The doubling of the word for the living is read two ways. Gill takes it of two kinds of life, since only the corporeally living can praise in this world and only the spiritually living can praise aright. Calvin uses the same doubling to restrict, denying that all men are meant, since many extinguish the glory of God by ingratitude; men, so long as God supports them here, may justly be regarded as the lawful heralds of his glory.

The clause about the father and the children yields the most unexpected observation here. Ellicott notes that the words are perfectly general, but take a particular force from the fact that the son who succeeded was only twelve at his father death, and so was not born until two or three years after this illness; the thought that there was no son to take his place may have added to the grief. He adds that the word rendered truth here means faithfulness rather than truth as an object of belief. Calvin draws a domestic rule from the same clause, that children are given on the express condition that each man shall labour by instructing them to transmit the name of God to posterity.

Two textual judgments stand beside this. Clarke records a variant in the particle before that word. Keil and Delitzsch make the larger claim, that the text here is not only curtailed but has fallen into confusion, since the two verses about the poultice and the sign have been removed from their proper place; they were dropped by oversight from the end of the earlier promise and added in the margin. They observe that even the oldest version keeps them at the close of the psalm.

On the last verse Calvin insists on the strength of the phrasing. To render it that it belongs to the Lord to save does not express enough; the king praises not only the power but the work in which it was proved, and having dreaded him as a severe judge now owns him as deliverer and leaps with joy. He adds why others are called in: a private man would still owe a public sacrifice, and a king far more, since in his person God had provided for the whole church. Ellicott would render the opening as a present rather than a past, and hears in the plural of the singing the king identifying himself with the congregation. Gill puts the reversal shortly: the man who one day expected death every moment was the next in the temple praising God.
21:
The two closing verses are agreed on all hands to stand out of place. Gill says the writing ends with the preceding verse and that these were added by the prophet or another hand, taken out of the parallel; he notes that one version supplies the name of the king as the person addressed, but thinks the direction was rather to some of the servants standing by. Keil and Delitzsch go further and refer the reader back to the earlier promise, holding that the two verses belong there and not here. Calvin reaches the same conclusion from the sense: some take the last verse as recording another sign and connect it with the one before as an exclamation of astonishment, but he thinks it more probable that the order has been reversed, as often with Hebrew writers, so that what was spoken last is related first. The prophet had not said at the outset that a sign was asked for, though the fuller history attests it, and so he adds at the end what he had passed over in its proper place.

The poultice of figs raises the question whether a remedy was used at all. Clarke has no doubt that it was, and that God in effecting the cure was pleased to order the use of means not improper for the end; he cites two ancient medical writers on figs applied to swellings and used to disperse what has gathered in a part of the body, and quotes an older rendering of one of them to the effect that the milky juice of the fig tree is of the same nature as vinegar and will curdle milk as rennet does, should be gathered before the figs are ripe and dried in the shade, and is then good to break an abscess.

Calvin reports the contrary opinion carefully before rejecting it. Some hold that this was no remedy at all, figs being hurtful in such a case, and that the plaster was applied precisely because it was unfitted to cure, so that the king might be taught openly that his recovery came from nothing but the favour of God. They compare the bow set in the cloud, which appears when thick clouds are gathering as though they would deluge the world, and yet was given as the pledge that it should not be drowned; a sign, on that view, may signify the opposite of what it seems to promise. Calvin answers that figs are used even by the physicians of his own day for bringing a swelling to a head, and thinks it likely that the Lord, having given a promise, gave a medicine along with it, as he has done on many other occasions. He does not need such means, but uses them when he sees fit; and the worth of the promise is not diminished by the plaster, which without the word would have been vain, since the king had already received another and supernatural sign by which he learned that the life he had despaired of came from God alone.

Calvin ends on what the question about going up to the house of God reveals of the man who asked it. His chief object throughout the added years was to celebrate the name of God; he had not desired life in order to live at ease, but to defend the honour of God and the purity of his worship. From that he draws the closing lesson, that God prolongs our lives not so that we may follow the bent of our natural disposition or give ourselves up to luxury, but that we may cultivate piety, perform kind offices to one another, and take our part often in the assembly of the godly and the public exercises of religion, so proclaiming the truth and goodness of God.
